idiom_name: Task running for await over an AsyncStream
implementation_notes: AsyncStream exists precisely to adapt callback- and delegate-based APIs to async-await, so the endpoint becomes a Task running for await message in stream { ... } over the transport's stream, calling the service (a plain actor or struct method) and writing the reply back through the transport's async send or a continuation. The continuation is Sendable, so a callback transport can yield from any context, and callback/delegate plumbing replaces the endpoint class. The classic callback-object structure is justified when the transport is purely delegate-based and cannot be adapted once at the edge.
pitfalls: AsyncStream's default buffering policy is unbounded: a service slower than the transport grows memory without limit; use bufferingPolicy: .bufferingNewest(n).
A cancelled Task ends the loop silently and buffered messages are dropped; check Task.isCancelled or call try Task.checkCancellation() before acknowledging.

The continuation and the service must be Sendable or actor-isolated: sharing a mutable class between the transport's callback context and the consuming task is a data race the compiler catches only when the types are annotated.
